snippet.title: NCAS Interview with Ben McKenzie, Director of "Everyone is Lying to You for Money"
snippet.description:
Ben McKenzie—actor, author, and now filmmaker—dives into cryptocurrency in his directorial debut Everyone is Lying to You for Money.

Best known for roles in The O.C. and Gotham, McKenzie has become a prominent critic of the crypto industry. He is also co-author of the book Easy Money: Cryptocurrency, Casino Capitalism, and the Golden Age of Fraud, which examines the rise of cryptocurrency and the risks it poses to investors and the broader financial system.

In this interview with National Capital Area Skeptics (NCAS) Board Member Jim Harris, McKenzie discusses his transition from curiosity about crypto to uncovering what he sees as systemic deception, misinformation, and financial exploitation. The conversation explores how Everyone is Lying to You for Money both educates and entertains while delivering a sharp critique of the crypto world.

Join NCAS members at the AFI Silver in downtown Silver Spring, Maryland, for special screenings of Ben's film on April 20, 2026 at 6:45 and April 25, 2026 at 6:15, both with Q&A with Ben McKenzie.  Details at https://www.ncas.org/2026/04/coming-april-20-and-april-25.html .

Views expressed in this video are those of the speakers and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Capital Area Skeptics.

snippet.title: The Age of Change | Why Humans Fear What We Evolved For
snippet.description:
Change feels unsettling. Uncomfortable. Sometimes even threatening.
But what if that feeling is not a flaw - and never was?
In this longform Sleepless Homo episode, The Age of Change, we explore how early humans survived a world that never stayed still. Long before cities, rituals, or identities, our ancestors lived inside constant environmental instability: shifting climates, vanishing resources, and landscapes that refused permanence.
  Through archaeology, paleoclimate science, evolutionary biology, and deep-time anthropology, this episode traces how change shaped human survival itself - not as a phase, but as a condition. You will hear how early humans learned when to leave, why tools were made to be abandoned, how memory replaced maps, and why fear of change evolved alongside adaptability.
This is not a video about self-improvement.
It is not about motivation, habits, or reinvention.It is about something older.
This episode is part one of a three-part Sleepless Homo series:

snippet.title: 1776: The Uncensored Story of The American Revolution
snippet.description:
Forget what you learned in school. Or from Hamilton. The American revolution was bigger and bloodier than you ever thought.

For the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, we bring you the undiscovered stories, heroes, and villains of the War for Independence. In this incredible six-part retelling, we go far beyond the 13 original colonies and the clash between American Patriots and British colonial troops. We traverse the Atlantic and plunge deep into the American West to discover a multi-front war that engulfed a diverse cast of characters – Indigenous people, enslaved Africans, American Loyalists, women of all social classes – and changed the face of world history.

EPISODE 1: UNLIKELY REVOLUTIONARIES 
We begin by profiling three unlikely revolutionaries: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and John Adams. 

EPISODE 2: REVOLUTION IN INDIAN COUNTRY 
When fighting breaks out between Britain and the American colonists, the native people of North America are forced to pick a side. 

EPISODE 3: THE SLAVES’ REVOLUTION
The American War for Independence was, in fact, two revolutions in one. There was the Revolution we know – of American Patriots against their British overlords. And there was the Revolution we don’t know – of enslaved Black people against their American overlords

snippet.description:

Hades was the Greek god of the underworld and one of the three brothers who divided the cosmos after the Titans fell. This full documentary covers the complete mythology of Hades, the Greek underworld, and the long history of how ancient Greek religion shaped the modern idea of Hell.

Topics covered include the origin of the underworld, the three gifts of the Cyclopes, the rivers Acheron and Styx, the judges of the dead, Charon the ferryman, Cerberus, Persephone, Orpheus and Eurydice, Sisyphus, Tantalus, Ixion, Theseus, Heracles, and the Chair of Forgetfulness.

The documentary also covers how the Greek god Hades became associated with the Christian concept of Hell through Septuagint translation, the word Sheol, Gehenna, and the Latin influence of Dis Pater and Pluto.

snippet.title: After the Bronze Age Collapse (1200 - 900 BC) | What Was Life Like in the First Dark Age?
snippet.description:
What was life like after the Bronze Age Collapse?
In this slow, cinematic documentary, we travel through the strange centuries that followed the fall of every major empire of the Late Bronze Age. Between twelve hundred and nine hundred years before the common era, the ancient world shattered - and yet, humanity rebuilt itself in quiet, resilient ways.
This episode explores:

• burned palaces, abandoned cities, and the long silence after empire
• climate shocks, failing crops, and the slow return of fields
• refugees, wanderers, pastoral clans, and the rise of new identities
• the first Iron Age villages, hillforts, kings, and micro-states
• how Egypt survived, fractured, and changed under Libyan dynasties
• the birth of Aram-Damascus and the pastoral kings
• how trade networks shrank but never died
• the first alphabetic experiments and the return of writing
• why the Iron Age began not in glory, but in small, stubborn acts of survival

Told softly, with scientific humility and firelight calm, this longform story guides you through one of the greatest transitions in human history - a world collapsing, and another quietly beginning.
If you enjoy deep time, archaeology, prehistory, ancient collapse, and slow storytelling, this episode is for you.

🕯️ The story of humanity… told softly.

• climate shocks, failing crops, and the slow return of fields
• refugees, wanderers, pastoral clans, and the rise of new identities

• how Egypt survived, fractured, and changed under Libyan dynasties
• the birth of Aram-Damascus and the pastoral kings
• how trade networks shrank but never died
• the first alphabetic experiments and the return of writing
• why the Iron Age began not in glory, but in small, stubborn acts of survival

Told softly, with scientific humility and firelight calm, this longform story guides you through one of the greatest transitions in human history - a world collapsing, and another quietly beginning.

For the 82nd anniversary of the D-Day Landings, this documentary brings back to life the 100 days it took for the Allies to liberate Normandy, to break through the German line and to pave the way towards victory. 100 critical days, both heroic and tragic, that made history.

“The free men of the world are marching together to Victory!” These are the words of Commander Eisenhower to the Allied troops on June 6, 1944. A few hours later, they were around 150,000 to land on the Normandy coast. Operation “Overlord” was launched: one of the largest military operations of the 20th century. D-Day: 100 Days for Freedom propels us into the 100 sensational days that followed, while reviving the experiences of soldiers on both sides.

 Broadcast in prime time, this film event retraces day by day – from D-Day up to the Liberation of Paris – this key moment of the Second World War, through a series of moving testimonies and spectacular colorized archives, both collective and intimate.

The story of the Inca Empire is pieced together from archaeology, oral tradition, and often conflicting Spanish accounts, but what emerges is the rise of the largest Indigenous empire in the Americas. From its legendary founder Manco Cápac to the transformative reign of Pachacuti, who turned Cusco into the heart of a vast imperial network stretching to Quito, the Inca built a highly organized state defined by monumental architecture, intricate labor systems, and knotted quipu record-keeping. Yet beneath this order, disease and dynastic rivalry fractured the empire after the death of Huayna Capac, sparking a brutal civil war between Atahualpa and Huáscar just as Francisco Pizarro arrived with steel, horses, and ambition. What followed was a dramatic collision of empires, where political calculation, greed, and resilience would determine the fate of the Andes.

📚  When you're done learning about the Inca Empire, head over to Incogni to take back your personal data! Just use code ExtraHistory at the link below and get 60% off annual plans: https://incogni.com/extrahistory

The story of the Inca Empire is pieced together from archaeology, oral tradition, and often conflicting Spanish accounts, but what emerges is the rise of the largest Indigenous empire in the Americas. From its legendary founder Manco Cápac to the transformative reign of Pachacuti, who turned Cusco into the heart of a vast imperial network stretching to Quito, the Inca built a highly organized state defined by monumental architecture, intricate labor systems, and knotted quipu record-keeping. Yet beneath this order, disease and dynastic rivalry fractured the empire after the death of Huayna Capac, sparking a brutal civil war between Atahualpa and Huáscar just as Francisco Pizarro arrived with steel, horses, and ambition. What followed was a dramatic collision of empires, where political calculation, greed, and resilience would determine the fate of the Andes.

snippet.title: Blaise Agüera y Arcas | What is Intelligence? | Long Now Talks
snippet.description:
Blaise Agüera y Arcas’s Long Now Talk took us on a journey through What is Intelligence?, his groundbreaking new work connecting the evolutionary dots between life, computation, and symbiogenesis. 

He explores how, in our symbiotic world, things combine to make larger things all the time. We might think of humanity in terms of the individual — but we're already part of everything we're creating, which is in turn co-creating us. 

In the story of technology and humanity, are we distinct from the technologies that we make? Agüera y Arcas' cuts through the essentialist dogma with a functionalist view: Biological computing — computation through DNA, RNA, and proteins — is not a strange outcropping of life but its very nature.

This talk was presented September 16, 02025 at the Cowell Theater in San Francisco. 
Episode notes: https://longnow.org/talks/02025-aguera-y-arcas/

The event livestream is here: https://www.youtube.com/live/NKxAWa7wKbU
    
This talk is part of Long Now Talks.

Launched by Stewart Brand in 02003, Long Now Talks has invited more than 400 leading thinkers to share their civilization-scale ideas with a live audience and millions around the globe tuning in to our podcast and videos. Long Now Talks are brought to you by The Long Now Foundation, which has spent the last 25 years igniting cultural imagination around long-term thinking.

By inspiring thought and conversation about how we've been shaped by the last 10,000 years and what might be in store for us over the next 10,000 years, Long Now Talks seek to expand our collective sense of the present moment. Long Now Talks cover futurism and speculative fiction; time, nature, and contemplative practices; the intersection of the humanities and sciences; the evolution of counterculture to cyberculture; cultural imagination, land art and public monuments; and of course, long-term thinking and being a good ancestor.

In our age of compounding crises, The Long Now Foundation is a counterweight. We are a force that imagines new possibilities, thinks critically, and takes action over the long term. Journey across the breathtaking frontiers of Tibet, Xinjiang and Yunnan — lands of towering mountains, ancient trade routes, hidden cultures and rapidly changing traditions. From the sacred monasteries of Tibet and the deserts of Xinjiang to the lush jungles of Yunnan, this epic Extra Long Edit explores the extraordinary people living on the edges of the modern Chinese world.

Discover remote ethnic minorities, ancient rituals, mysterious festivals, breathtaking landscapes and ambitious modern development transforming some of the most isolated places on Earth.

snippet.title: Born From Darkness: The Solar Child and the Oldest Myth Humans Ever Told
snippet.description:
Born From Darkness: The Solar Child and the Oldest Myth Humans Ever Told is a quiet, archaeological journey into one of humanity’s oldest narrative patterns - the moment when early people looked at the fading winter sun and imagined it as a fragile child returning from darkness.
 This slow, sleep-friendly documentary explores how myths of rebirth, light, and midwinter vulnerability arose independently across the world long before organized religion. From circumpolar darkness and prehistoric carvings to Indo-European, Andean, Celtic, and Near Eastern traditions, we trace how ancient storytellers turned the sky into meaning. The “solar child” - the weak, newborn light - appears in cultures separated by oceans, climate, and time. Why?
 Archaeology, anthropology, linguistics, and comparative mythology all point toward the same answer: humans learned to narrate the world by watching the year’s most fragile moment. This is not a video about belief or faith. It’s about deep time, human cognition, and the oldest story shape we ever recognized. For sleepless minds, late-night thinkers, and anyone who listens to long-form science to relax - welcome back to the firelight.

🕯️ The story of humanity… told softly.

snippet.title: Vlad the Impaler: The Monster Behind the Myth
snippet.description:
🎬 WATCH AD-FREE & SUPPORT THE CHANNEL:
YouTube demonetized this channel but still runs ads on every video, meaning they profit from your views while I earn nothing. On Patreon you watch everything ad-free, and your support goes directly to keeping these documentaries alive.
➡️ Join here: https://patreon.com/FadingLore

Vlad the Impaler was the 15th-century Wallachian prince whose reign of terror inspired the Dracula legend.
This documentary explores Transylvania, the Ottoman Empire, Sultan Mehmed II, and the empty tomb at Snagov Monastery.

In 1442, an eleven-year-old boy was handed over to the Ottoman Empire as a hostage. For five years, he watched executions, learned the art of impalement, and witnessed his brother become a favorite of the future Sultan. When news arrived that his father had been assassinated and his elder brother buried alive, something inside that boy died. Something else was born.

Vlad III Dracula returned to Wallachia with a single purpose: vengeance. He massacred the nobility who had betrayed his family. He built forests of impaled bodies to terrorize his enemies. When Sultan Mehmed II, the conqueror of Constantinople, invaded with 90,000 soldiers, Vlad struck his camp at midnight with 7,000 cavalry. The assassination attempt failed. The terror succeeded. Mehmed found 20,000 bodies on stakes blocking the road to the capital. He turned back. The man who conquered a thousand-year empire could not conquer Vlad.

This is the true history behind the vampire legend. A story of hostages and assassinations, of night attacks and psychological warfare, of a prince whose empty tomb still puzzles archaeologists. The voivode died in 1477. Dracula has never died at all.

snippet.title: 11. Byzantium - Last of the Romans (Part 2 of 2)
snippet.description:
On the outskirts of modern Istanbul, a line of ancient walls lies crumbling into the earth...

In this episode, we look at one of history’s most incredible stories of survival - the thousand-year epic of the Byzantine Empire. Find out how this civilization suffered the loss of its Western half, and continued the unbroken legacy of Rome right through the middle ages. Hear about how it formed a bridge between two continents, and two ages, and learn how the impregnable walls of Constantinople were finally brought crashing to the ground. 

This episode we're joined by members of the St Sophia Greek Orthodox Cathedral Choir in London, and a number of musicians playing traditional Byzantine instruments.

snippet.title: Unit 731: The Crime America Decided Was Too Useful to Punish
snippet.description:
Unit 731 was the largest program of human experimentation of the Second World War. Most people have never heard of it, and that is not an accident.
In nineteen forty-seven, the United States hanged German doctors at Nuremberg for experimenting on human beings. At the very same moment, on the other side of the world, it was secretly granting immunity to the Japanese doctors who had done far worse, in exchange for the data from their experiments. This is the documented story of that bargain: how America chose to protect the architects of Unit 731 rather than prosecute them, why it did so, and what the decision cost long after the war was over.
This is not a catalogue of atrocities. It is an investigation into a choice, drawn from declassified cables, the records of the Tokyo War Crimes Tribunal, and the 1998 admission by the U.S. Department of Justice that it had "essentially assisted Japan in covering up" what the unit had done. Where the record is firm, this film states it plainly. Where claims are contested — the true value of the data, the death tolls, the allegations that resurfaced during the Korean War — it says so, and explains why the uncertainty itself is part of the story.

Powell, John W. "A Hidden Chapter in History." Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, vol. 37, no. 8, October 1981. — The article that first exposed the cover-up to an American audience.

snippet.title: A Discussion of "How to Talk to a Science Denier" (Lee McIntyre, PhD)
snippet.description:
For our March event, NCAS invites you to read the book "How to Talk to a Science Denier" BEFORE March 11, 2023. Then join us on Saturday, March 11 at 1:30 PM ET for an online Q & A with author Lee McIntyre.

Think of it as the ultimate book club meeting...your friends and acquaintances show up to discuss a book, and the author shows up too!

From the book's website:

"Can we change the minds of science deniers? Encounters with flat earthers, anti-vaxxers, coronavirus truthers, and others.

'Climate change is a hoax—and so is coronavirus.' 'Vaccines are bad for you.' These days, many of our fellow citizens reject scientific expertise and prefer ideology to facts. They are not merely uninformed—they are misinformed. They cite cherry-picked evidence, rely on fake experts, and believe conspiracy theories. How can we convince such people otherwise? How can we get them to change their minds and accept the facts when they don't believe in facts? In this book, Lee McIntyre shows that anyone can fight back against science deniers, and argues that it's important to do so. Science denial can kill.

Drawing on his own experience—including a visit to a Flat Earth convention—as well as academic research, McIntyre outlines the common themes of science denialism, present in misinformation campaigns ranging from tobacco companies' denial in the 1950s that smoking causes lung cancer to today's anti-vaxxers. He describes attempts to use his persuasive powers as a philosopher to convert Flat Earthers; surprising discussions with coal miners; and conversations with a scientist friend about genetically modified organisms in food. McIntyre offers tools and techniques for communicating the truth and values of science, emphasizing that the most important way to reach science deniers is to talk to them calmly and respectfully—to put ourselves out there, and meet them face to face."

https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262545051/how-to-talk-to-a-science-denier/

snippet.title: The ENTIRE Story of Colonial America – Full Detailed Documentary
snippet.description:
Journey through the entire story of colonial America in this full educational documentary. From powerful Indigenous nations and early European encounters to the rise of English colonies and the road to revolution, this video walks you through the major turns that shaped a new world.
We explore Spanish and French ambitions, the struggle and survival of Jamestown, the tobacco boom in the Chesapeake, Puritan visions in New England, and the diverse Middle Colonies built on trade and toleration. You will see how slavery and the Atlantic world created the plantation South, and how everyday colonial life was shaped by law, religion, and empire.
The documentary also covers the Great Awakening, the French and Indian War, and the growing clash between British imperial reforms and colonial demands for rights. Step by step, you will understand how protests over taxes, boycotts, and British troops in Boston led to open conflict at Lexington and Concord.
This video is designed for students, history fans, and anyone who wants a clear, engaging, and fact based overview of colonial America from first contact to the eve of independence.

snippet.title: Everything You Wanted to Know About Coronaviruses But Were Afraid to Ask (Laura Kahn, MD, MPH,MPP)
snippet.description:
Using an interdisciplinary One Health approach, Dr. Laura Kahn will draw upon material from her book, "One Health and the Politics of Covid-19," to talk about the history, science, research, and politics of coronaviruses. One Health is the concept that human, animal, plant, environmental, and ecosystem health are linked. This is a relatively new term, but an ancient concept recognized by indigenous peoples around the world.

Coronaviruses are zoonotic viruses, meaning that they originate in non-human animals (i.e., bats) and spread to humans. The most well-known coronaviruses are Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS), Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), and Covid-19. Unlike SARS and MERS, which emerged in 2002 and 2012, respectively, Covid-19 appears unusual in some of its clinical manifestations. The gold standard evidence used to prove the natural origins of the earlier coronavirus epidemics is lacking with Covid-19. The origin of this virus remains controversial.

Coronaviruses were first discovered by veterinarians in the early 1930s. Physicians discovered them in the 1960s while studying “the common cold” but assumed that they were merely nuisance microbes. Medical researchers lost interest in them until the shocking appearance of SARS. Gain-of-function research of pandemic potential pathogens, such as SARS, and the possibility that it might have led to Covid-19, raises concerns about the ethics and risks of this type of research.

Dr. Laura H. Kahn is a physician, policy researcher, educator, and author. For almost 20 years, she was a research scholar in the Program on Science and Global Security at Princeton's School of Public and International Affairs, Princeton University. Her education and training encompass nursing, medicine, public health, and public policy.

A native of California, Dr. Kahn holds a bachelor's degree in nursing from UC Los Angeles, a doctorate in medicine from the Mt. Sinai School of Medicine, a master's degree in public health from Columbia University and a master's degree in public policy from Princeton University. Dr. Kahn is a fellow of the American College of Physicians. In 2007, the New Jersey Chapter of the American College of Physicians awarded her with their highest honor, the Laureate Award. In 2014, the American Association of Public Health Physicians awarded her with a Presidential Award for Meritorious Service, and in 2016, the American Veterinary Epidemiology Society (AVES) awarded her with their highest honor for her work in One Health: the K.F. Meyer-James H. Steele Gold Head Cane Award.

Views expressed in this presentation are those of the speaker and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Capital Area Skeptics.

snippet.title: The Wild Hunt: The Story That Haunted Every Winter for 1,000 Years
snippet.description:
🎬 WATCH AD-FREE & SUPPORT THE CHANNEL:

For a thousand years, across every culture that endured northern winters, people looked up at the dark December sky and heard the same thing: hoofbeats. Horns. Howling hounds. They called it by different names: Odin's Ride, the Maisnie Hellequin, the Cŵn Annwn but the message was always the same: stay inside, don't look up, and pray they pass you by.

In this documentary, we trace the Wild Hunt from the chronicles of medieval monks to the video games of the 21st century. We meet Odin, the one-eyed god who led the dead across Scandinavian skies. We hear the Hounds of Annwn, whose baying grows quieter the closer they come. We follow King Herla, cursed to ride forever because a bloodhound never jumped from its horse.

We explore how Christianity transformed a pagan procession into a demonic warning and how the terror of Hellequin became the comedy of Harlequin. We discover echoes of the Wild Hunt in our Christmas traditions, in our modern paganism, and in games like The Witcher 3.

The Wild Hunt is the oldest story humanity told about what lives in the darkness above. This is that story, from its ancient roots to its digital rebirth.

snippet.title: POV: You Live in Europe’s Tallest, Filthiest "Skyscrapers" (Edinburgh, 1750) #shorts #history
snippet.description:
Before Edinburgh’s New Town, much of the city lived vertically.

In the Old Town, people were packed into tall stone tenements rising above narrow closes and wynds. The wealthy, the poor, lawyers, servants, vendors, students, and laborers all squeezed through the same stairs, lanes, and dark passages.

Sanitation was brutal. Many homes had no private plumbing, so dirty water and waste often went into the street gutters below. That is where the famous warning “Gardyloo!” comes from, shouted before slops were thrown from above.

But this was not some forgotten village. This was Edinburgh during the Scottish Enlightenment, a city of law, learning, taverns, print, trade, poverty, smoke, and overcrowding all stacked on top of each other.

Brilliant minds upstairs. Filth running underneath.
#edinburgh #historical

snippet.title: 19. The Mongols - Terror of the Steppe
snippet.description:
In the far east of the Eurasian steppe, the sound of hoofbeats is growing...

In this episode we travel along the vast grassland corridor of the steppe, to hear one of the most remarkable and unlikely stories from medieval history – the story of the Mongol Empire. Find out how this group of nomadic horse riders united the peoples of the Mongolian steppe, and forged them into a truly unique kind of state. Discover how they conquered much of the lands of Eurasia, and brought the distant cultures of China, Persia, the Middle East and Europe into contact. And hear the story of how the world’s largest land empire finally came apart, and left the world as we know it in its wake.

You know it as a harmless holiday decoration, a reason to steal a kiss in a doorway. But for thousands of years, mistletoe was the most feared and revered object in the European forest. This documentary peels back the red ribbon to reveal the "Sacred Parasite". A plant that ancient civilizations believed was the literal key to the Underworld and the only weapon capable of killing the sun.

Our journey begins in the Roman myths of the Aeneid, where the "Golden Bough" serves as a glowing passport for the hero Aeneas to descend into Hell alive. We then travel north to the frozen forests of Iron Age Gaul, reconstructing the terrifying "Ritual of the Oak and Sickle," where Druids harvested the plant with golden blades and paid for it with the blood of white bulls. Finally, we uncover the tragedy of the Prose Edda, where the trickster Loki weaponizes the plant’s innocence to assassinate Baldur the Beautiful, triggering the Norse apocalypse.
